voiceNote: One female narrator with a neutral American accent for every clip: calm, confident, measured. Generated once with scripts/generate-narration.mjs; see docs/NARRATION.md.

items.title: Welcome
items.text: Welcome to Afuq. We’re approaching the Moon’s south pole. Pick a site, then move through time to see when the Sun and Earth clear the local horizon.
items.speech: Welcome to Ah-fooq. We’re approaching the Moon’s south pole. Pick a site, then move through time to see when the Sun and Earth clear the local horizon.

items.title: The Moon and its south pole
items.text: This is the Moon, shown with imagery from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. Near the south pole the Sun never climbs far above the horizon, so long shadows shape the landscape. Some crater floors here never receive direct sunlight, and they are cold enough to hold water ice. Nearby rims and peaks, by contrast, can stay sunlit for much of the year. NASA has named nine candidate regions for the Artemis Three landing. This app measures, from real terrain data, when each of them can see the Sun and the Earth.

items.title: Peak near Cabeus B
items.text: Peak near Cabeus B is a candidate region on high ground near the crater Cabeus B, about eighty-four degrees south. Its neighbor, the crater Cabeus, is where NASA's LCROSS mission struck the Moon in 2009 and detected water in the material it threw up. At the observation point this app uses inside NASA's outline, the center of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-eight percent of 2027.

items.title: Haworth
items.text: The Haworth region lies on terrain beside Haworth crater, about fifty-one kilometers across, whose floor is permanently shadowed. At roughly thirty kilometers across, its outline is one of the larger ones NASA has drawn. At the observation point this app uses, the center of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-six percent of 2027.

items.title: Malapert Massif
items.text: Malapert Massif is part of Mons Malapert, a broad mountain about sixty-seven kilometers across, named after the seventeenth-century astronomer Charles Malapert. It sits on the Earth-facing side of the south pole, so from its high ground the Earth is often above the horizon. At the observation point this app uses, the center of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about sixty-three percent of 2027.

items.title: Mons Mouton Plateau
items.text: Mons Mouton Plateau is the largest of the nine outlines, roughly seventy-eight by fifty-eight kilometers, across the high and comparatively flat top of Mons Mouton. The mountain is named after Melba Roy Mouton, a NASA mathematician and programmer. At the observation point this app uses, the center of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-five percent of 2027.

items.title: Mons Mouton
items.text: The Mons Mouton region is a smaller outline on the same mountain, on its slopes to the west of the large crater Nobile. Its high ground gives long views over the surrounding terrain. At the observation point this app uses, the center of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about sixty-seven percent of 2027, the highest share among the nine points.

items.title: Nobile Rim 1
items.text: Nobile Rim One lies on the western rim of Nobile, a crater about seventy-nine kilometers across, named after the Italian polar explorer Umberto Nobile. Crater rims near the pole rise into sunlight while the crater floor stays in shadow. At the observation point this app uses, the center of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about sixty-four percent of 2027.

items.title: Nobile Rim 2
items.text: Nobile Rim Two lies on the northern side of the same crater, Nobile, farther from the pole than Rim One. At the observation point this app uses, the center of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-one percent of 2027, the lowest share among the nine points.

items.title: de Gerlache Rim 2
items.text: de Gerlache Rim Two is on the rim of de Gerlache, a crater about thirty-three kilometers across, named after the Belgian polar explorer Adrien de Gerlache. At about eighty-eight degrees south, it is the closest of the nine regions to the pole. At the observation point this app uses, the center of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about fifty-eight percent of 2027.

items.title: Slater Plain
items.text: Slater Plain is a comparatively smooth area near Slater crater, about twenty-five kilometers across, named after the planetary scientist David Slater. It lies on the side of the pole facing away from the Earth's usual direction, so the Earth is often close to its horizon. At the observation point this app uses, the center of the Sun clears the measured skyline for about sixty-two percent of 2027.

items.title: Standing on the surface
items.text: You are standing at the observation point, two meters above the ground. The terrain all the way to the horizon is built from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter measurements, so the skyline you see is the measured skyline. The Sun and the Earth are drawn at their true directions and sizes. The fine ground texture, the lifted shadows and the soft glow around the Sun and the Earth are display aids, not measurements. You can switch them off in the layers menu.

items.title: Reading Mission Analysis
items.text: Mission Analysis compares two places over a period you choose. Sun above the skyline is the share of time the center of the Sun is visible, which matters for solar power and warmth. Earth above the skyline is the share of time the Earth is in geometric line of sight. That is needed for direct communication, but it does not guarantee a working link. The longest stretch without Sun shows how long equipment would have to last in darkness. Every result applies to one observation point, and slopes, hazards and operations are not modeled.

items.title: Elevation
items.text: Elevation is the angle of an object above the local horizontal plane. Zero degrees is level with the eye, and ninety degrees is straight overhead. Near the south pole the Sun's elevation stays within a few degrees of the horizon all year.

items.title: Azimuth
items.text: Azimuth is the compass direction of an object, measured clockwise from local north, which points toward the Moon's north pole. East is ninety degrees, south is one hundred and eighty, and west is two hundred and seventy.

items.title: Terrain skyline
items.text: The terrain skyline is the highest angle of the surrounding ground in a given direction. Here it is traced through NASA's LOLA elevation data out to one hundred and fifty kilometers. A body is hidden whenever its elevation is below the skyline, even if it is above the horizontal.

items.title: Clearance
items.text: Clearance is a body's elevation minus the skyline in its direction. A positive value means the center of the Sun or the Earth is above the terrain. A negative value means the terrain hides it.

items.title: Observation coordinates
items.text: The coordinates give the observation point's latitude and longitude on the Moon, with east counted positive. The point is chosen by a fixed rule inside NASA's region outline. It is a representative point for these calculations, not a NASA landing site.

items.title: Visibility intervals
items.text: A visibility interval is a period in which a body stays above the skyline without interruption. The timelines draw them as bars. The longest gap without the Sun shows how long a landed system would face darkness.

items.title: Observation time
items.text: Observation time is in Coordinated Universal Time. The arrows step back or forward by an hour or a day. Open the date to choose any moment inside the period covered by the JPL ephemeris. Play moves time forward at one hour, six hours, or one day per second, and every reading updates as it goes.

items.title: Display options
items.text: Display options choose what is drawn. Measured layers come from NASA data, such as the LOLA skyline, the directions to the Sun and the Earth, and LROC surface brightness. Display aids, such as labels, grids, range rings, and lifted shadows, make the scene easier to read and are not measurements. In Surface View, the Survey, Landscape, and Physical presets set common combinations.

items.title: Measurements
items.text: Measurements lists the full readings for the Sun and the Earth from the observation point: elevation above level ground, azimuth from local north, the height of the terrain skyline in that direction, the clearance between them, and how much of the disc is above the skyline. The lower part describes the observation point and its NASA region.

items.title: Data and method
items.text: Data and method lists every source this app uses: NASA's nine Artemis Three candidate regions, JPL Horizons for the Sun and the Earth, LOLA terrain, LROC imagery, and the Yale Bright Star Catalogue. It also reports how the calculations were validated. This is a Space Apps project, not an official NASA product.

items.title: All candidate regions
items.text: This list shows all nine candidate regions with their NASA imagery and the current state of the Sun and the Earth at each observation point. Choose one to select it on the globe.

items.title: Choosing scenarios
items.text: Each scenario is one candidate region, a start date in Coordinated Universal Time, and a duration. Choose the region from its name, type or pick the start date, and select a preset duration or one from More durations. Both scenarios are calculated the same way, so the differences come from the place and the period.

items.title: At a glance
items.text: At a glance compares the two scenarios on four questions: how much of the period the Sun is above the skyline, how much the Earth is, how often both are, and the longest stretch without the Sun. Each row shows both values and the difference. When the longest dark stretch touches the start or the end of the period, it is a lower bound, so no winner is declared.

items.title: Through time
items.text: The timelines show, for each scenario, when the Sun and the Earth are above the measured skyline. Each bar is an uninterrupted interval of visibility. Hover, or use the arrow keys, to read exact values, and click or press Enter to pin a moment and open it in the 3D views.

items.title: From the ground
items.text: These panoramas show the measured skyline all the way around each observation point, with the paths of the Sun and the Earth over the period. Solid dots are above the skyline, and hollow dots are hidden by terrain. Each scenario can be exported as a CSV file from here.

items.title: Every metric
items.text: Every metric lists ten measures side by side, with the difference between the scenarios. Percentages are shares of the period. Values marked greater than or equal to are lower bounds, because the interval reaches the edge of the period, and their differences are shown as not applicable.

items.title: Method and limits
items.text: The Sun and Earth directions come from NASA JPL Horizons, and they agree with Horizons to better than a hundredth of a degree. The skyline is traced through LOLA terrain data out to one hundred and fifty kilometers. Visible means the center of the disc is above the skyline. Results apply to one observation point, and slopes, hazards, temperatures, and radio links are not modeled.

items.title: The Moon from orbit
items.text: This is the Moon, as NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has mapped it. Everything in this app is built from NASA measurements: orbital imagery, laser altimetry of the terrain, and JPL ephemerides for the Sun and the Earth.

items.title: Moving around
items.text: Drag to turn the globe, and scroll or pinch to zoom. The buttons on the right zoom in and out, return to the selected region, or show the whole Moon. Double-click a point to fly toward it. Press F at any time to hide the controls and focus on the scene.

items.title: The lunar south pole
items.text: We are now above the lunar south pole. Here the Sun skims the horizon, so high ground can stay sunlit while deep craters stay dark. The outlines mark NASA's nine candidate regions for Artemis Three.

items.title: Choosing a region
items.text: This is Malapert Massif, one of the nine regions. You can choose any region from the panel on the left. The dot marks the observation point this app measures from. It is a representative point chosen by a fixed rule inside NASA's outline, not a NASA landing site.

items.title: Observation time
items.text: The bar at the bottom sets the observation time, in Coordinated Universal Time. Step by an hour or a day, open the date to choose any moment in the covered period, or press play to watch the light change at one hour, six hours, or one day per second.

items.title: Sun and Earth measurements
items.text: The panel on the right reports the Sun and the Earth as seen from the observation point. Elevation is the angle above level ground. A body counts as visible only when its center is above the measured terrain skyline, not just above the horizontal. Sunlight matters for power and warmth. A line of sight to Earth is needed for direct communication.

items.title: Surface View
items.text: Now we stand on the surface, two meters above the observation point. The terrain out to the horizon comes from NASA's laser altimeter, so the skyline you see is the measured skyline. The Sun and the Earth are drawn at their true directions and sizes.

items.title: Surface controls and layers
items.text: Drag to look around. The buttons on the right turn you to face the Sun, the Earth, or north, and change the field of view. The strip at the bottom shows the whole horizon at once. Display options switch aids such as labels, the skyline line, and enhanced lighting on or off.

items.title: Mission Analysis
items.text: Mission Analysis compares two scenarios. Each one is a region, a start date, and a duration. Every fifteen minutes, or every hour for periods longer than sixty days, the Sun and the Earth are checked against the measured skyline.

items.title: Comparing scenarios
items.text: At a glance shows how often each body is visible, and the longest stretch without the Sun. When a dark stretch touches the start or the end of the period, its full length is unknown. It is marked as a lower bound, and no winner is declared. A longer period can settle the comparison.

items.title: CSV exports
items.text: Each scenario can be exported as a CSV file, with the Sun and Earth directions, the skyline height, and visibility at every time step. The file header lists the data sources. Use it to check the results or to analyze them further.

items.title: Data, methods, and limits
items.text: Data and method lists every source: NASA's LOLA terrain, LROC imagery, and JPL Horizons ephemerides, and how the results were validated. Results apply to one observation point. Slopes, hazards, temperatures, and radio links are not modeled, and this is not an official NASA product. That is the end of the tour.
